name: Esther Farah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me, Esther. I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to companies, unions or government. What you tell me stays confidential. Can you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I drive a grader at Saltbush, a big open-pit lithium mine out on the flats. My job is keeping the haul roads smooth and properly cambered, which means tilted so water runs off, because a rough road chews through tyres that cost more than my car. Twelve-hour shifts, mostly days. I like it because the road is never finished, and a good road makes the whole pit run faster.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The boredom on a quiet night, and the heat in summer when the aircon in the cab struggles. Also being one of four women on my crew, which is fine most days, but you notice it. I live on my own in a flat in town that I bought two years ago, so on my days off it's just me, the gym and a lot of podcasts.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Do you use technology much, at work or outside it?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: All the time. I use an AI assistant every day, for budgeting, for planning my training, even to explain the road design specs the engineers send. Last month I asked it to help me work out why the same corner on Ramp 3 keeps rutting, and I took the answer to the road engineer. Saltbush has an autonomous haul truck trial running, and I put my name down to help with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ha. I'd be a bit disappointed, to be honest. I like the stuff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the tools are still handy even if they're not magic. I'd probably post something like, the robots aren't coming for the grader just yet. At work I'd keep showing people the little tricks, like getting the AI to read the pre-start faults.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, that's a pretty safe life. Lithium demand is strong, I'm on good pay, and there are other mines around if Saltbush has a bad year. I'd just keep building my savings and my skills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going on the grader and keep pushing to get on the autonomous truck trial, because even a slow trial is a skill. I'd keep putting a third of my pay into an index fund and the flat. And I'd probably do a short course in mine surveying, just because I'm curious.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a bit flat. It's the steady version of my life, which isn't a bad thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that would worry you in this version, money-wise?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Lithium prices dip sometimes, and last year Saltbush cut a night crew. But I've got about a year of costs saved and my flat's half paid off. Even if they cut my crew, I'd have work at Cooper Flats or the gold mine up the road within weeks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: So what would bother you most about this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably the boredom. If nothing changes, I'm grading the same ramps at thirty-five. I'd want a bigger job by then. Maybe road design or a supervisor role.

say: The tools are **still handy**, even if they're not magic.
The robots aren't coming for **the grader** just yet.
think: **Lithium demand** and good pay make this a safe life for her.
With a **year saved**, a crew cut wouldn't hurt for long.
do: Keep pushing to join the **autonomous truck trial** at Saltbush.
Put a **third of her pay** into an index fund and the flat.
Sign up for a **short course** in mine surveying.
feel: **Calm** and a little flat, as this is the steady version of her life.
S0.quote: If nothing changes, I'm grading the same ramps at thirty-five. I'd want a bigger job by then.
fieldNote: Her main risk here is **boredom**, not money or job loss.
She already uses AI **every day**, so a plateau feels like a letdown, not relief.
Strong savings and **nearby mines** make her genuinely secure.

steps.text: Keep grading haul roads and apply for the truck trial
Put a third of each pay into an index fund
Take a short mine surveying course at the local college

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the one I've been expecting, honestly. And I think I'm ready for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, don't fight it, learn it. At smoko I'd be the annoying one telling people to sign up for the remote operations training. Online I'd post about what the trial is actually like, because most people have no idea.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think it's good for me. The thinking jobs shrink first, the planners and the purchasing people, and the grader stays mine for a while. By the time the robots spread to hands-on work, I want to be the person running them from a screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get on the autonomous truck trial and then go for a remote operator role in the operations centre, which pays about the same without the dust. I'd use the AI to study the fleet software in my own time, maybe ten hours a week. And I'd start a small online guide for operators learning these systems, as a side thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited, mostly. A little guilty, because some of my crew won't like it, and I'll look like I'm cheering it on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on your crew would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dougie (my crew's leading hand) has been grading for twenty-five years and hates screens. I'd worry about him, and the older truckies. I'd offer to sit with him and go through the simulator, but I can't make him do it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me more about this online guide. Is it about money?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The online guide would just be short videos, how the fleet software works, what the alarms mean. If it made a few hundred a month, great, but mostly it's to get my name known for when the remote jobs open up.

say: Don't fight it, **learn it**, and sign up for remote training.
She'd post about what the **autonomous trial** is really like.
think: The **planners and buyers** feel it first; the grader stays hers for now.
She wants to be the one **running robots** from a screen.
do: Move from the truck trial into a **remote operator** role in the operations centre.
Study the **fleet software** with AI for about ten hours a week.
Start a **short-video guide** for operators learning the systems.
feel: Mostly **excited**, with some **guilt** about how her crew sees her.
S1.quote: By the time the robots spread to hands-on work, I want to be the person running them from a screen.
fieldNote: She sees this picture as an **opportunity** and has a concrete path to take it.
Her worry is for **older crew** like Dougie, not for herself.
The side guide is about **reputation** more than money.

steps.text: Apply for a remote operator role in the operations centre
Study the autonomous fleet software ten hours a week
Post short videos explaining fleet alarms for new operators

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay, that changes things. Two years is not enough for anyone, including me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it out loud: the companies will love this and the workers will get told about it last. I'm not anti-AI, I use it every day. But I'd say we need the mine to share some of what it saves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, my remote operator plan stops working. If AI can do almost any thinking job by 2028, it can watch a screen better than I can. The grader itself probably lasts until the robots come, so I've got about five years of real work. After that I'm not sure what a person like me does in mining.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd grab the remote operator job anyway in year one, because it pays and it puts me close to the systems. Then I'd work out which jobs need a human body on site, like fixing and checking the robots, and train for that, probably a heavy diesel fitter's ticket. I'd keep my savings untouched and stop putting money into the index fund until I know what's happening to shares.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not scared for next year, I'll be fine next year. Scared for thirty-two-year-old me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you talk to about it first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably my mum, who thinks I'm the sensible one. I'd tell Mum the truth, that I don't know, but that I've got a year saved and I'm not going to sit still.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you stop spending on?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The holiday to Japan I've been saving for, sadly. And the extra mortgage payments. I'd want cash where I can reach it.

say: Workers will **hear last** while the companies welcome it.
The mine should **share some** of what it saves.
think: Her **remote operator** plan fails once AI can watch screens itself.
She expects about **five years** of grader work before robots arrive.
do: Take the **remote operator** job in year one for pay and access.
Train toward a **heavy diesel fitter** ticket for on-site robot work.
Pause the **index fund** and extra mortgage payments, and hold cash.
feel: **Anxious** about her future at thirty-two, though fine for next year.
S2.quote: I'm not anti-AI, I use it every day. But I'd say we need the mine to share some of what it saves.
fieldNote: Even the **early adopter** loses her plan here; the thinking side goes first.
She still uses the **three-year robot gap** to pick a trade.
Her shift from investing to **holding cash** shows real worry under a calm voice.

steps.text: Take the remote operator job in the operations centre
Start a heavy diesel fitter apprenticeship for on-site work
Stop index fund payments and keep cash in savings
Cancel the Japan holiday and the extra mortgage payments

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is better. I can do a lot in five years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I said about the slow one, learn it, but now with a deadline. I'd push my crew to do courses while the company is still paying for them. Online I'd probably write about it a lot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd get maybe three good years as a remote operator, then the AI takes that, and then the grader goes around 2034. That's eight years of mining pay. Enough to pay off the flat and build a real cushion.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the remote job, pay off the flat by 2030, and start studying something that needs hands and judgement together, probably maintenance on the autonomous fleet. I'd keep the online guide going and see if it grows. And I'd keep investing, but spread out, not all in one fund.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. It's a real change, but I can see a road through it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you leave town for work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably yes, if the work went. I've got no kids, the flat's paid off by then, I could rent it out and go where the robot maintenance jobs are.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You love AI and it's taking your job. How do you square that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd have to fight myself on that. I'm the one who loves this stuff, and it's still taking my job. Those two things can both be true.

say: Learn it, but **with a deadline**, while the company pays for courses.
She'd **write a lot** online about what is happening on site.
think: About **eight years** of mining pay is enough to clear the flat.
Remote work lasts **three years** before AI takes that too.
do: Pay off the **flat by 2030** from remote operator pay.
Study **autonomous fleet maintenance**, which needs hands and judgement.
feel: **Uneasy**, but she can see a road through it.
S3.quote: I'm the one who loves this stuff, and it's still taking my job. Those two things can both be true.
fieldNote: She names her own **contradiction** before anyone else does.
Being **single, no kids** and owning the flat makes moving easy for her.
Five years moves her from **anxious to uneasy**.

steps.text: Pay off the flat by 2030 with remote operator pay
Study autonomous fleet maintenance at the college
Rent out the flat and move to where robot maintenance jobs are

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's a whole career change with time to spare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the best case, and people should stop panicking and start planning. I'd tell the young ones to do a trade that works next to the robots. Online I'd be the optimist, as usual.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'm fine. Ten years from now I'm thirty-seven, I'll have been through remote ops and something after that. The question is what I want to be doing, not whether I'll eat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the remote operator job, then use the company's study support to do a two-year diploma in automation engineering, which is the people who design and set up these systems. I'd invest steadily. And I'd buy a second small flat to rent, because people still need somewhere to live.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Curious, even.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the trap for you in this version?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Thinking it's far away and staying on the grader too long. That's the classic mistake. I'd put a date on it, 2030 at the latest, to be off the machine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And outside of your own plans, what would bother you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably still the guilt about the older crew. Dougie will be close to retiring, so he'll be fine, but the people in their forties will be stuck in the middle.

say: This is the **best case**, so plan instead of panic.
Young miners should do a **trade next to** the robots.
think: At thirty-seven she'll have moved through **remote ops** and beyond.
The question is **what she wants**, not whether she'll eat.
do: Use company study support for a **two-year diploma** in automation engineering.
Buy a **second small flat** to rent out.
feel: **Calm** and curious about what comes next.
S4.quote: The question is what I want to be doing, not whether I'll eat.
fieldNote: Ten years turns this into a **career choice** for her, not a threat.
She knows her trap is **staying too long** on the grader.
Her worry moves to **workers in their forties** stuck in the middle.

steps.text: Do a two-year automation engineering diploma with company support
Buy a second small flat in town to rent out
Leave the grader for remote operations by 2030

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. I'm the one who's ahead, and even I don't have a plan that survives two years. What would help is if the mine had to give notice and fund training before they switch things on, not after, and if there were real apprenticeships for robot maintenance in mining towns.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask whether I'd want to stay in mining at all. Maybe not. The robots might be the push I need to do something I'd choose for myself.

headlineQuote: I'm the one who's ahead, and even I don't have a plan that survives two years.
portrait: Esther, 27, drives a **grader** on the haul roads at Saltbush, an open-pit lithium mine.
She lives alone, owns a **flat** half paid off, and has a year saved.
She uses **AI every day** and has signed up for the autonomous truck trial.
Slow change excites her, but **AGI by 2028** breaks even her remote operator plan.
With **ten years** she'd move into automation engineering and buy a rental flat.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because even her plan doesn't survive two years.
whatWouldHelp: Mines giving **notice and training** before switching systems on.
Real **robot maintenance apprenticeships** in mining towns.
